quote.short: The snapshot of a security's current trading state: last price, change, bid/ask, volume and the day's range.
quote.long: A quote is the summary a data provider sends for a symbol at a moment in time. It usually includes the last traded price, the previous close, the change since then, the day's open, high and low, and the volume traded so far. Every number in a quote has a timestamp, and on free data plans that timestamp can be minutes old.
quote.example: AAPL 189.50 +2.10 (+1.12%), Vol 41.2M, Range 186.90 to 190.05: last trade 189.50, up 2.10 from yesterday's close of 187.40.
quote.pitfalls: A quote is not a promise of a fill price. Check the timestamp before treating it as live.

ticker.short: The short code that identifies a security on an exchange, like AAPL, SPY, BTC-USD or WALMEX.MX.
ticker.long: Tickers are unique per exchange, not worldwide. The same company can trade under different tickers on different exchanges, and a suffix such as .MX, .TO or .L often tells you which exchange. Crypto and currency pairs use both currency codes, for example BTC-USD or EURUSD.
ticker.example: Walmart de Mexico is WALMEX.MX on the Mexican exchange (BMV); Walmart Inc. is WMT on the NYSE. They are different companies with different prices.
ticker.pitfalls: Similar tickers can belong to unrelated companies. Confirm the company name before adding a symbol.

exchange.short: A regulated marketplace where securities are listed and traded, such as the NYSE, Nasdaq, BMV or B3.
exchange.long: An exchange sets the trading hours, holidays and listing rules for what trades on it. Prices you see come from trades reported on one or more venues. Each exchange runs on its own time zone, so 'market open' depends on which exchange you are looking at.
exchange.example: The NYSE regular session is 9:30 to 16:00 New York time, which is 7:30 to 14:00 in Mexico City for most of the year.
exchange.pitfalls: Daylight-saving changes happen on different dates in different countries, so the gap between your clock and the exchange's can shift by an hour for a few weeks.

last-price.short: The price of the most recent reported trade. It is what most apps call 'the price'.
last-price.long: The last price is a record of what someone actually paid on the latest trade, not what you would pay right now. In a quiet stock the last trade can be minutes old while the bid and ask have moved. Providers may also report the last price from a single venue instead of the whole market.
last-price.example: Last 52.10 at 14:31:05. If the current ask is 52.30, buying now would cost about 52.30, not 52.10.
last-price.pitfalls: On thinly traded symbols the last price can be stale. Compare it with the bid/ask and the quote time.

bid.short: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay. Sellers who sell immediately get roughly the bid.
bid.long: The bid is the top of the buy side of the order book. If you sell at market, you trade against bids, starting with the best one. The bid size tells you how many shares are wanted at that price.
bid.example: Bid 99.95 x 300 means buyers want 300 shares at 99.95.
bid.pitfalls: Many free data plans do not include bid/ask at all, and outside regular hours the bid can be far from the last price.

ask.short: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept. Buyers who buy immediately pay roughly the ask.
ask.long: The ask is the top of the sell side of the order book. A market buy order trades against the ask, and larger orders may walk up to higher asks. Ask size tells you how many shares are offered at that price.
ask.example: Ask 100.05 x 200 means sellers offer 200 shares at 100.05.
ask.pitfalls: In fast or illiquid markets the ask can jump between the moment you look and the moment an order reaches the market.

spread.short: The gap between the ask and the bid. It is a hidden cost you pay every time you trade in and out.
spread.long: The spread is the difference between the lowest ask and the highest bid. Heavily traded large companies often have spreads of a cent; small companies, options, some ETFs and after-hours sessions can have much wider ones. A round trip (buy, then sell) costs roughly one full spread on top of commissions.
spread.example: Bid 9.90, ask 10.10: the spread is 0.20, or 2% of the price. Buying and immediately selling 100 shares would lose about 20 before fees.
spread.pitfalls: Percent spread matters more than the cents. A 0.05 spread is tiny on a 500 stock and large on a 2 stock.

prev-close.short: The official closing price of the last regular session. Daily change is measured from it.
prev-close.long: The previous close is set by the exchange at the end of the regular session, often through a closing auction. Change and percent change for the day are calculated against it. After a split or special dividend, providers adjust it so the change stays meaningful.
prev-close.example: Previous close 50.00 and last 51.50: change +1.50, percent change +3.00%.
prev-close.pitfalls: Some providers use the last after-hours trade instead of the official close, so different apps can show slightly different daily changes.

change.short: Last price minus the previous close, in currency units.
change.long: Change tells you how far the price has moved since the last regular-session close. It is positive when the price is higher and negative when lower. It says nothing about the reasons for the move.
change.pitfalls: Absolute change is hard to compare between symbols with different prices. Use percent change for comparisons.

pct-change.short: Change divided by the previous close, as a percentage. It lets you compare moves across symbols.
pct-change.long: Percent change = (last - previous close) / previous close x 100. It is the standard way to compare how much different symbols moved, whatever their price. Watchlists usually sort and colour by it.
pct-change.example: A 2.40 drop from 120.00 is -2.00%. A 2.40 drop from 24.00 would be -10.00%.
pct-change.pitfalls: A -50% move needs +100% to recover. Percent losses and gains are not symmetric.

open-price.short: The price of the first trade (or opening auction) of the regular session.
open-price.long: The open is set when the regular session starts. The difference between the open and the previous close is the gap. Comparing the current price to the open shows how the stock has done during today's session alone.
open-price.example: Prev close 40.00, open 41.00, last 40.20: up 0.50% on the day but down about 1.95% from the open.
open-price.pitfalls: Pre-market trades are not the open. The open belongs to the regular session.

pct-from-open.short: How far the price has moved since today's regular-session open, as a percentage.
pct-from-open.long: Change from open isolates what happened during the session itself, separating it from the overnight gap. A stock can be up on the day and still be falling from its open. Alerts on this measure watch intraday moves.
pct-from-open.pitfalls: Before the open it has no meaning; the alert waits until a regular-session open exists.

day-range.short: The lowest and highest prices traded during the current session.
day-range.long: The day range shows how much the price has swung today. Where the last price sits inside the range hints at how the session is going: near the high means buyers have held control, near the low means sellers have. A wide range compared with normal days signals higher volatility.
day-range.example: Range 98.20 to 103.40 with last 103.10: the price is near the top of today's range.
day-range.pitfalls: Some providers include extended-hours trades in the range and others do not.

volume.short: The number of shares (or units) traded in a period. It shows how much activity is behind a price move.
volume.long: Volume counts how many shares changed hands. A move on heavy volume involved many participants, while a move on light volume can reverse more easily. Daily volume resets each session, so it is naturally low early in the day.
volume.example: A stock that usually trades 2M shares a day trades 6M today while rising 5%: three times its normal activity.
volume.pitfalls: Comparing today's partial volume with a full day's average overstates how quiet the morning is. Crypto volume is spread across many exchanges and is rarely complete.

avg-volume.short: The typical daily volume over a lookback, often 10 days or 3 months.
avg-volume.long: Average volume gives the baseline for 'normal' activity in a symbol. It is also a rough liquidity gauge: very low average volume usually means wider spreads and bigger jumps. Different providers use different lookbacks.
avg-volume.example: Avg volume (3M) 1.8M: on a typical day about 1.8 million shares trade.
avg-volume.pitfalls: One huge news day can inflate a short average for weeks.

relative-volume.short: Current volume divided by average volume. Above 1 means busier than usual.
relative-volume.long: Relative volume puts today's activity in context. Values of 2 or more often accompany news, earnings or index changes. Intraday, a fair comparison scales the average to the time of day, because most volume trades near the open and close.
relative-volume.pitfalls: Early in the session, a plain full-day RVOL is misleadingly low. High RVOL says activity is unusual, not which way the price will go.

liquidity.short: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. High volume and tight spreads mean good liquidity.
liquidity.long: A liquid security has many buyers and sellers at prices close together, so orders fill near the quoted price. Illiquid securities can have wide spreads, sudden gaps and difficulty exiting a position. Liquidity also falls in pre-market, after-hours and holiday sessions.
liquidity.example: An S&P 500 ETF trading tens of millions of shares a day with a 0.01 spread is very liquid; a microcap trading 20,000 shares with a 0.15 spread is not.
liquidity.pitfalls: Liquidity disappears when you need it most, in a panic or a crash.

market-cap.short: Share price times shares outstanding: what the market values the whole company at.
market-cap.long: Market cap is a size measure. Roughly, large caps are above 10 billion USD, mid caps 2 to 10 billion and small caps below 2 billion, though the cut-offs vary by source. Size affects volatility, liquidity and which indexes a stock belongs to.
market-cap.example: Price 50 x 400M shares = 20 billion market cap.
market-cap.pitfalls: Market cap is not the company's cash or sale price; it ignores debt. A low share price does not mean a company is small or cheap.

shares-outstanding.short: The total number of a company's shares held by all shareholders, including insiders.
shares-outstanding.long: Shares outstanding change when a company issues new stock (dilution), buys back stock or splits. It is used to calculate market cap and per-share figures like EPS. Dilution means each existing share owns a smaller slice of the company.
shares-outstanding.example: A company with 100M shares issues 10M more: existing holders now own 10% less of it per share.
shares-outstanding.pitfalls: Data can lag a recent offering or buyback by a quarter.

float.short: Shares actually available to trade publicly, excluding those locked up by insiders and large holders.
float.long: The float is usually smaller than shares outstanding. A small float means a small supply of tradable shares, which can make the price move sharply on modest buying or selling. Index providers often weight by float.
float.example: 500M shares outstanding with 350M held by the founders: float is roughly 150M.
float.pitfalls: Low-float stocks are prone to extreme swings and are a frequent target of hype.

market-session.short: The time window when an exchange accepts trades: pre-market, regular, after-hours, or closed.
market-session.long: Each exchange defines its sessions in its own local time. Most volume and the official open and close happen in the regular session. This app works out the session from your device clock and a local holiday table, and labels it when it cannot be sure.
market-session.example: NYSE: pre-market from 4:00, regular 9:30 to 16:00, after-hours to 20:00, all New York time.
market-session.pitfalls: A wrong device clock or time zone makes every session label wrong.

regular-session.short: The main trading hours of an exchange, when liquidity is highest and official open and close prices are set.
regular-session.long: The regular session runs between the opening and closing auctions. Daily candles, daily change and most indicators are built from regular-session data. Alerts in this app can be restricted to the regular session.
regular-session.example: BMV (Mexico) regular session: 8:30 to 15:00 Mexico City time.
regular-session.pitfalls: Half days before some holidays close early.

pre-market.short: Trading before the regular open. Prices react to overnight news but liquidity is thin.
pre-market.long: Pre-market trading happens on electronic venues before the official open. Fewer participants means wider spreads and prices that can swing more than they would during the day. Pre-market prices do not set the official open.
pre-market.example: A company reports earnings at 7:00; the stock trades +6% pre-market on light volume and opens +3%.
pre-market.pitfalls: A big pre-market move on tiny volume often shrinks or reverses at the open. Many free providers do not report pre-market quotes.

after-hours.short: Trading after the regular close. Earnings often come out then, so moves can be large on little volume.
after-hours.long: After-hours (post-market) trading runs on electronic venues after the close. Like pre-market, it has thin liquidity and wide spreads. The previous close stays the reference until the next regular session.
after-hours.example: Close 80.00; after earnings the stock trades at 74.00 after-hours, -7.5% on a few hundred thousand shares.
after-hours.pitfalls: Your app's 'change' may or may not include after-hours trades, depending on the provider.

extended-hours.short: Pre-market plus after-hours: trading outside the regular session.
extended-hours.long: Extended hours cover both sides of the regular session. Many brokers allow only limit orders then, because prices can be erratic. Data providers vary a lot in whether, and how quickly, they report extended-hours prices.
extended-hours.example: A stock alert set to 'regular only' ignores a spike to 120 at 18:30.
extended-hours.pitfalls: Thin markets make extended-hours highs and lows unreliable reference points.

trading-halt.short: A temporary stop in trading of one stock or a whole market, ordered by the exchange or regulator.
trading-halt.long: Halts happen for pending news, for big price swings (volatility pauses, called circuit breakers when market-wide) or for regulatory reasons. While halted, the last price freezes. Trading usually resumes with an auction, sometimes at a very different price.
trading-halt.example: A stock is halted at 12.00 for news; it reopens 25 minutes later at 15.50.
trading-halt.pitfalls: A frozen price during a halt can look like a calm market. This app flags quotes whose timestamp stops advancing as stale.

market-holiday.short: A weekday when an exchange is closed. Holidays differ by country and exchange.
market-holiday.long: Exchanges publish their holiday calendars in advance, plus occasional early closes. A US holiday is not a Mexican or Brazilian holiday, so markets can be open in one country and closed in another. This app ships a holiday table with a horizon and marks dates it cannot vouch for.
market-holiday.example: US markets close on Thanksgiving, while BMV in Mexico is open; Mexico closes on 16 September, while US markets are open.
market-holiday.pitfalls: Unscheduled closures (national mourning, outages) are not in any holiday table.

stock.short: A unit of ownership in a company. Its price reflects what buyers and sellers think the company is worth.
stock.long: Owning a share gives you a claim on part of a company's assets and earnings, and usually voting rights. Shareholders benefit through price gains and dividends, and can lose their whole investment if the company fails. Stock prices move with company results, interest rates, the economy and sentiment.
stock.example: Buying 10 shares at 25 costs 250 plus fees. If the price rises to 30, the position is worth 300.
stock.pitfalls: A single stock can drop far more than the overall market.

etf.short: A fund that trades on an exchange like a stock and usually holds a basket of securities, often tracking an index.
etf.long: An ETF lets you buy many securities in one trade. Most track an index such as the S&P 500, but some are actively managed, leveraged or inverse. ETFs charge an annual expense ratio that is taken out of the fund's value.
etf.example: An S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio costs about 3 per year for every 10,000 invested.
etf.pitfalls: Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily and can lose value over time even when the index ends flat. Read what an ETF actually holds.

expense-ratio.short: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of what you have invested.
expense-ratio.long: The expense ratio is deducted from the fund's assets continuously, so you never see a bill; it shows up as slightly lower returns. Over decades, small differences compound into large amounts. Index ETFs tend to be cheaper than actively managed funds.
expense-ratio.example: 100,000 invested for 20 years at 7%/yr: with a 0.05% fee it grows to about 384,000; with a 1.00% fee to about 321,000.
expense-ratio.pitfalls: Expense ratio is not the only cost: spreads, trading commissions and taxes add up too.

index.short: A calculated number that tracks a group of securities, such as the S&P 500, Nasdaq-100 or S&P/BMV IPC.
index.long: An index measures how a market or a segment is doing. You cannot buy an index directly, but you can buy funds that track one. Indexes differ in how they weight members: by market cap, by price, or equally.
index.example: SPY is an ETF that tracks the S&P 500 index; the market strip often uses SPY, QQQ and DIA as stand-ins for the big US indexes.
index.pitfalls: A cap-weighted index can rise because of a handful of giant companies while most members fall.

adr.short: A certificate traded in the US that represents shares of a foreign company.
adr.long: ADRs let US-market investors hold foreign companies in dollars during US hours. One ADR may represent several or a fraction of the underlying shares. Its price follows the home-market share converted at the exchange rate, plus small fees.
adr.example: If one ADR equals 2 home shares worth 100 MXN each and USD/MXN is 18.00, the ADR should trade near 2 x 100 / 18 = 11.11 USD.
adr.pitfalls: ADRs carry currency risk and sometimes custody fees deducted from dividends.

crypto.short: A digital asset recorded on a blockchain, traded 24/7 on many exchanges at slightly different prices.
crypto.long: Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ether have no central exchange or closing time. Prices are quoted against a currency or stablecoin (BTC-USD, ETH-USDT). They are far more volatile than most stocks and have no earnings or dividends in the usual sense.
crypto.example: A 10% daily move in a major cryptocurrency is unusual but not rare; for a large US stock it would be exceptional.
crypto.pitfalls: There is no official 'close'; providers pick a cut-off (often 00:00 UTC) for daily change, so numbers differ between sources.

stablecoin.short: A crypto token designed to hold a steady value, usually 1 US dollar.
stablecoin.long: Stablecoins aim to keep their peg through reserves of cash and bonds, or through crypto collateral and algorithms. They are used as a dollar stand-in on crypto exchanges. A stablecoin is only as stable as the assets and the issuer behind it.
stablecoin.example: USDT and USDC usually trade between 0.998 and 1.002 USD.
stablecoin.pitfalls: Several stablecoins have lost their peg, some permanently. They are not bank deposits.

fx-pair.short: The price of one currency in another, such as USDMXN: how many Mexican pesos one US dollar buys.
fx-pair.long: In a pair, the first currency is the base and the second is the quote. USDMXN at 18.50 means 1 USD = 18.50 MXN. If USDMXN rises, the dollar strengthened against the peso. FX markets trade around the clock on weekdays.
fx-pair.example: USDMXN goes from 18.00 to 18.90: the dollar rose 5% against the peso; a peso holder's US investments are now worth 5% more in pesos.
fx-pair.pitfalls: EURUSD and USDEUR are inverses. Check which way round a pair is before reading its direction.

pip.short: The standard small step in a currency price: 0.0001 for most pairs, 0.01 for pairs quoted in yen.
pip.long: Pips make FX moves easy to talk about. Many pairs are quoted with an extra decimal (a fractional pip). The value of one pip in money depends on the size of the position.
pip.example: EURUSD from 1.0850 to 1.0875 is a 25-pip move. USDJPY from 150.20 to 150.45 is also 25 pips.
pip.pitfalls: USDMXN is quoted to four decimals, so its pip is 0.0001 even though the price is near 18.

candlestick.short: A chart bar showing open, high, low and close for one period. The body spans open to close; wicks reach the high and low.
candlestick.long: A candle is filled or coloured up (often green) when the close is above the open, and down (often red) when it closes below. Long wicks show prices that were reached but rejected. Each candle's period depends on the chart's timeframe: one minute, one day, one week and so on.
candlestick.example: Open 100, high 106, low 98, close 104: an up candle with a body from 100 to 104, an upper wick to 106 and a lower wick to 98.
candlestick.pitfalls: A candle's colour compares close with open, not with the previous close. A green candle can still be a down day.

ohlc.short: Open, High, Low, Close: the four prices that summarise trading in one period.
ohlc.long: OHLC data is the raw material of most charts and indicators. An OHLC bar chart draws each period as a vertical line from low to high, with a tick on the left for the open and one on the right for the close. Adding volume makes it OHLCV.
ohlc.pitfalls: OHLC hides the path within the bar; you cannot tell whether the high or the low came first.

heikin-ashi.short: Smoothed candles built from averages of the real ones, so trends look cleaner. They are not real traded prices.
heikin-ashi.long: Each Heikin-Ashi close is the average of the bar's open, high, low and close; each open is the midpoint of the previous Heikin-Ashi candle's body. The result filters noise and makes runs of same-coloured candles more common during trends. The trade-off is that the displayed prices differ from actual prices.
heikin-ashi.example: A real close of 104 can show as a Heikin-Ashi close of 102 for the same bar.
heikin-ashi.pitfalls: Never read prices or set levels from Heikin-Ashi candles; switch back to normal candles to see real values.

line-chart.short: Charts that connect closing prices with a line. Simple and good for seeing the overall direction.
line-chart.long: A line chart plots one value per period, usually the close. An area chart fills the space below the line, and a baseline chart colours it above or below a reference such as the previous close. They hide intraperiod highs and lows, which makes them less noisy for beginners.
line-chart.example: A 1-year line chart of daily closes shows 250 or so points joined together.
line-chart.pitfalls: Because highs and lows are hidden, a line chart can understate how volatile a period was.

timeframe.short: The period each bar covers (1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day) and the span the chart shows (1D, 1Y, MAX).
timeframe.long: The interval sets how much time each candle represents, and the range sets how far back the chart goes. The same stock can look like it is rising on a daily chart and falling on a 5-minute chart. Indicators are calculated per bar, so a 14-period RSI means 14 minutes on a 1-minute chart and 14 days on a daily one.
timeframe.example: Range 5D with 15-minute bars gives about 130 bars for a US stock (26 per day).
timeframe.pitfalls: Free data plans often limit intraday history or return fewer bars than requested.

log-scale.short: A price axis where equal distances mean equal percentage changes, not equal amounts.
log-scale.long: On a linear scale, a move from 10 to 20 looks tiny next to 100 to 110 later on, even though the first doubled the price. On a log scale, every doubling takes the same vertical space. Log scale is the fairer view for long histories and for fast-growing assets.
log-scale.example: On a log chart, 10 to 20 (+100%) and 100 to 200 (+100%) are the same height.
log-scale.pitfalls: Trendlines drawn on a log chart do not line up with the same lines on a linear chart.

gap.short: When a bar opens away from the previous close, leaving an empty space on the chart. Today's gap = open vs previous close.
gap.long: Gaps happen when news arrives while the market is closed, such as earnings or economic data. A gap up opens above the previous high or close; a gap down opens below. Some gaps fill, meaning price comes back to the previous close; others mark the start of a lasting move.
gap.example: Prev close 50.00, open 53.00: a +6.0% gap up.
gap.pitfalls: Stop-loss orders do not protect against gaps: a stop at 48 can fill at 44 if the stock opens there.

trend.short: The general direction of price over a period: up (higher highs and higher lows), down, or sideways.
trend.long: An uptrend is a series of higher highs and higher lows; a downtrend is the reverse. Trends exist on every timeframe and can disagree with one another. Moving averages and trendlines are common ways to make a trend visible.
trend.example: Daily lows of 90, 94 and 97 with highs of 100, 105 and 109 describe an uptrend.
trend.pitfalls: Trends are obvious in hindsight and ambiguous in real time. A trend can end without warning.

trendline.short: A straight line drawn along swing lows (uptrend) or swing highs (downtrend) to visualise a trend.
trendline.long: A trendline connects at least two points and is extended forward. Traders watch for price respecting the line or breaking through it. Because people pick the points, two people can draw different lines on the same chart.
trendline.example: Connect the lows at 94 (March) and 97 (May) and extend the line to see where it would sit in July.
trendline.pitfalls: Trendlines are subjective and behave differently on log and linear scales.

support-resistance.short: Price zones where falling prices have tended to stop (support) or rising prices have tended to stall (resistance).
support-resistance.long: Support and resistance come from memory: many participants remember where they bought, sold or got stopped out. Round numbers, previous highs and lows, and moving averages often act as these zones. When resistance breaks, it sometimes becomes support, and the other way round.
support-resistance.example: A stock bounced near 50 three times this year; 50 is a support zone. It has failed near 62 twice; 62 is resistance.
support-resistance.pitfalls: They are zones, not exact lines, and they eventually break.

breakout.short: A move through a resistance (or below a support) level that had held before.
breakout.long: A breakout means price escaped a range it had been stuck in. Breakouts on high volume are generally considered more meaningful than ones on low volume. Many breakouts fail and fall back into the range, which is called a false breakout.
breakout.example: Resistance at 62; the stock closes at 64 on 2.5x average volume.
breakout.pitfalls: Intraday pokes through a level often reverse by the close. Waiting for a close beyond the level filters some of them.

volume-profile.short: A side histogram showing how much volume traded at each price level over a period.
volume-profile.long: Unlike normal volume bars, which are plotted over time, a volume profile is plotted over price. Prices with heavy trading (high-volume nodes) often act as support or resistance, and thin areas tend to be crossed quickly. The level with the most volume is called the point of control.
volume-profile.example: Over 3 months, 40% of all volume traded between 48 and 51: that zone is a high-volume node.
volume-profile.pitfalls: It needs detailed intraday data to be accurate; built from daily bars it is only an approximation.

moving-average.short: The average price over the last N bars, recalculated each bar. It smooths noise to show the trend.
moving-average.long: A moving average 'moves' because the oldest bar drops off as each new bar arrives. Short averages (10, 20) react quickly; long ones (50, 200) are slow and show the bigger trend. The common types are simple (SMA), exponential (EMA) and weighted (WMA).
moving-average.example: The 50-day SMA is the average of the last 50 daily closes.
moving-average.pitfalls: All moving averages lag price. They describe what happened; they do not predict.

sma.short: The plain average of the last N closes. Every bar counts equally.
sma.long: SMA = sum of the last N closes / N. The 50-day and 200-day SMAs are widely followed: price above the 200-day is often described as a long-term uptrend. An SMA reacts slowly, and also jumps when a big old bar drops out of the window.
sma.pitfalls: Needs N bars before it has a value; on short histories long SMAs simply do not appear.

ema.short: A moving average that gives more weight to recent prices, so it reacts faster than an SMA.
ema.long: The EMA applies a multiplier k = 2 / (N + 1) to the newest close and (1 - k) to the previous EMA. Recent bars dominate, but every past bar still has a little influence. The 12- and 26-period EMAs are the building blocks of MACD.
ema.example: N = 9 gives k = 0.2. Previous EMA 50, new close 55: EMA = 0.2 x 55 + 0.8 x 50 = 51.
ema.pitfalls: Faster reaction also means more false signals in choppy markets. Early values depend on how the EMA was seeded.

wma.short: A moving average that weights bars linearly: the newest counts N times, the oldest once.
wma.long: WMA = (N x newest + (N - 1) x next + ... + 1 x oldest) / (N(N + 1) / 2). It sits between the SMA and EMA in responsiveness and, unlike the EMA, completely forgets bars older than N.
wma.pitfalls: Same lag caveats as any moving average.

vwap.short: The average price of the session weighted by volume. It resets each day on intraday charts.
vwap.long: VWAP adds up price x volume for every bar of the session and divides by total volume, using the typical price (high + low + close) / 3. It shows the average price paid by everyone today. Institutions use it as an execution benchmark, and many intraday traders treat it as a fair-value line.
vwap.pitfalls: It only makes sense on intraday charts with real volume. On daily bars or with missing volume it is meaningless.

bollinger-bands.short: A moving average with bands 2 standard deviations above and below. The bands widen when volatility rises.
bollinger-bands.long: The default uses a 20-period SMA and bands at plus and minus 2 standard deviations of the closes. Narrow bands (a squeeze) mark quiet periods that are often followed by bigger moves. A close outside a band means the move was large compared with recent volatility.
bollinger-bands.example: SMA 50, standard deviation 1.5: upper band 53, lower band 47.
bollinger-bands.pitfalls: Touching a band is not a sell or buy signal; in strong trends price can ride a band for weeks.

keltner.short: An EMA with bands set a multiple of ATR above and below. Smoother than Bollinger Bands.
keltner.long: Keltner Channels typically use a 20-period EMA with bands at plus and minus 2 x ATR(10). Because ATR includes gaps and ranges, the channel reacts to volatility differently from Bollinger Bands. When Bollinger Bands fall inside the Keltner Channel, some traders call it a squeeze.
keltner.example: EMA 100, ATR 2.5, multiplier 2: bands at 105 and 95.
keltner.pitfalls: Settings vary by platform (some use SMA or a different ATR period), so values may not match other tools exactly.

donchian.short: Lines at the highest high and lowest low of the last N bars, with a midline between them.
donchian.long: The Donchian Channel shows the recent trading range. A close above the upper line means a new N-bar high, which is the basis of classic breakout systems such as the 20-day breakout. The channel steps rather than curving.
donchian.example: Highest high of the last 20 days 58, lowest low 49: channel 49 to 58, midline 53.5.
donchian.pitfalls: Breakouts from the channel fail often in sideways markets.

ichimoku.short: A Japanese indicator system with five lines and a shaded cloud that summarise trend, momentum and support.
ichimoku.long: Ichimoku uses a conversion line (Tenkan, 9-period midpoint), a base line (Kijun, 26-period midpoint), two leading spans plotted 26 bars ahead that form the cloud (Kumo), and a lagging span (Chikou) plotted 26 bars back. Price above the cloud is read as an uptrend, below as a downtrend, inside as no clear trend.
ichimoku.example: Tenkan = (highest high + lowest low) / 2 over 9 bars; with high 110 and low 100, Tenkan = 105.
ichimoku.pitfalls: It is dense and easy to over-read. The default 9/26/52 settings come from a six-day trading week and are not universal.

psar.short: Dots above or below price that trail a trend and flip sides when the trend reverses.
psar.long: SAR stands for Stop And Reverse. The dots accelerate towards price as a trend continues, using an acceleration factor that starts at 0.02 and grows by 0.02 per new extreme up to 0.20. When price crosses the dots, they flip to the other side.
psar.example: In an uptrend the dot sits at 95 under a price of 100; if price falls to 94.80, the dots jump above price.
psar.pitfalls: In sideways markets it flips constantly and produces many false reversals.

supertrend.short: A single line, based on ATR, that sits below price in uptrends and above it in downtrends.
supertrend.long: Supertrend starts from the bar midpoint (high + low) / 2 and adds or subtracts a multiple of ATR, commonly 3 x ATR(10). The line only moves in the trend's direction until price closes through it, and then it flips. It is popular as a visual trend filter and trailing reference.
supertrend.example: Midpoint 100, ATR 2, multiplier 3: lower band 94; it stays at or above 94 while the uptrend lasts.
supertrend.pitfalls: Like any trend follower it lags, and it whipsaws in ranges.

rsi.short: A 0 to 100 momentum gauge comparing recent gains with recent losses. Above 70 is often called overbought, below 30 oversold.
rsi.long: RSI = 100 - 100 / (1 + RS), where RS is the average gain divided by the average loss over N bars (default 14), smoothed with Wilder's method. It measures the speed of price changes, not value. It is not related to 'relative strength' versus another symbol.
rsi.example: Average gain 1.20 and average loss 0.60 over 14 days: RS = 2, RSI = 100 - 100 / 3 = 66.7.
rsi.pitfalls: 'Overbought' is not 'about to fall': in strong uptrends RSI can stay above 70 for a long time.

macd.short: The gap between a 12- and a 26-period EMA, with a 9-period signal line and a histogram of their difference.
macd.long: MACD line = EMA(12) - EMA(26). The signal line is a 9-period EMA of the MACD line, and the histogram is MACD minus signal. Crosses of MACD over its signal line, and crosses of zero, are read as momentum shifts.
macd.example: EMA12 = 52.4, EMA26 = 51.0: MACD = 1.4. If the signal is 1.1, the histogram is +0.3.
macd.pitfalls: Built from two lagging averages, it signals late and gives many crosses in sideways markets. Values are in price units, so they are not comparable across symbols.

stochastic.short: Shows where the close sits within the last N bars' high-low range, from 0 to 100.
stochastic.long: %K = (close - lowest low) / (highest high - lowest low) x 100, usually over 14 bars, and %D is a 3-period average of %K. Readings above 80 mean the close is near the top of the recent range, below 20 near the bottom. Crosses of %K and %D are watched as momentum turns.
stochastic.pitfalls: It reaches extremes easily in trends and can stay there.

stoch-rsi.short: The stochastic formula applied to RSI values instead of prices. Very sensitive, from 0 to 100 (or 0 to 1).
stoch-rsi.long: StochRSI measures where the current RSI sits within its own range over the last N bars. It moves between extremes much more often than RSI. It is usually smoothed with %K and %D lines.
stoch-rsi.example: RSI over 14 bars ranged 40 to 70 and is now 64: StochRSI = (64 - 40) / 30 = 0.80, or 80.
stoch-rsi.pitfalls: Its sensitivity means many signals and many false ones.

atr.short: The average size of each bar's full range, including gaps. A pure volatility measure in price units.
atr.long: True range is the largest of: high - low, |high - previous close| and |low - previous close|. ATR averages it over N bars (default 14, Wilder smoothing). It says how much the price typically moves per bar, not which direction. It is widely used to size stops and positions.
atr.example: ATR(14) = 2.30 on a 60 stock means a typical daily swing of about 3.8%.
atr.pitfalls: ATR is in currency units, so compare symbols using ATR / price.

adx.short: Measures how strong a trend is (0 to 100), whatever its direction. +DI and -DI show which side is stronger.
adx.long: ADX is built from directional movement: +DI rises when highs are expanding, -DI when lows are expanding, and ADX smooths the gap between them. ADX above roughly 25 is often read as a trending market and below 20 as a range. +DI above -DI suggests upward pressure.
adx.pitfalls: A falling ADX means the trend is weakening, not reversing. It reacts slowly.

obv.short: A running total that adds volume on up days and subtracts it on down days.
obv.long: OBV turns volume into a cumulative line. Its absolute value means nothing; its direction is what matters. Traders compare OBV's trend with price: if price rises but OBV falls, the rise has less volume behind it.
obv.example: OBV 1,000,000; today closes up on 200,000 shares: OBV becomes 1,200,000.
obv.pitfalls: One huge-volume day can dominate the line for months.

mfi.short: A volume-weighted RSI from 0 to 100, using typical price times volume.
mfi.long: MFI compares money flowing in on up bars with money flowing out on down bars over N periods (default 14). Readings above 80 or below 20 are commonly treated as extremes. Because it includes volume, it can differ from RSI on high-volume days.
mfi.example: Positive money flow 6M, negative 2M: ratio 3, MFI = 100 - 100 / 4 = 75.
mfi.pitfalls: Needs reliable volume; crypto and FX volume data are often partial.

cci.short: How far the typical price is from its average, scaled by mean deviation. Values beyond +/-100 are notable.
cci.long: CCI = (typical price - SMA of typical price) / (0.015 x mean deviation), usually over 20 bars. The 0.015 constant makes most readings fall between -100 and +100. Despite the name it works on any market.
cci.example: Typical price 105, its 20-bar SMA 100, mean deviation 2.5: CCI = 5 / 0.0375 = 133.
cci.pitfalls: It has no upper or lower bound, so extreme values can keep getting more extreme.

williams-r.short: Where the close sits in the last N bars' range, on a -100 to 0 scale. It is the stochastic %K flipped.
williams-r.long: %R = (highest high - close) / (highest high - lowest low) x -100, typically over 14 bars. Readings from -20 to 0 are near the top of the range and -100 to -80 near the bottom.
williams-r.pitfalls: Same limitation as the stochastic: extremes can persist in trends.

roc.short: Percent change of the close compared with N bars ago.
roc.long: ROC = (close - close N bars ago) / close N bars ago x 100. It oscillates around zero: positive means higher than N bars ago. It is the simplest momentum measure and is easy to compare across symbols.
roc.example: Close 110 today, 100 twelve days ago: ROC(12) = +10%.
roc.pitfalls: The value depends heavily on what happened on the one bar N periods back.

cmf.short: Averages where each close fell within its bar, weighted by volume, over N bars. Ranges from -1 to +1.
cmf.long: For each bar, the money flow multiplier is ((close - low) - (high - close)) / (high - low), from -1 for a close at the low to +1 at the high. CMF sums multiplier x volume over N bars (default 20) and divides by total volume. Positive values suggest closes near the highs on volume.
cmf.pitfalls: It ignores gaps between bars, so a big gap down with a close near the bar's high still reads positive.

volume-ma.short: An average of volume over N bars, drawn over the volume bars to show what is normal.
volume-ma.long: A volume MA (often 20 or 50 bars) makes spikes easy to see: bars well above the line had unusual activity. It is the basis of relative volume.
volume-ma.example: 20-day volume MA 1.5M; today's bar at 4.5M is three times the average.
volume-ma.pitfalls: Holiday sessions and half days distort it briefly.

pivot-points.short: Support and resistance levels calculated from the previous period's high, low and close.
pivot-points.long: Classic pivot P = (high + low + close) / 3; R1 = 2P - low, S1 = 2P - high, with further levels outward. Fibonacci and Camarilla variants use different multipliers. Many intraday traders watch them because so many others do.
pivot-points.pitfalls: They are mechanical levels with no knowledge of news or trend.

fibonacci.short: Horizontal lines at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of a move, used to look for pullback levels.
fibonacci.long: You pick a swing low and swing high, and the tool draws levels at those ratios of the distance between them. Traders watch whether a pullback stalls near a level. The ratios come from the Fibonacci sequence, except 50%, which is included by convention.
fibonacci.example: Move from 100 to 150: the 38.2% retracement is 150 - 0.382 x 50 = 130.90; 61.8% is 119.10.
fibonacci.pitfalls: With five levels, price almost always reacts near one of them, which makes the tool look better in hindsight than it is.

relative-strength.short: One symbol's price divided by another's, such as a stock versus its index. A rising line means it is outperforming.
relative-strength.long: Relative strength compares performance rather than measuring momentum. Dividing a stock by SPY shows whether it is beating the market. It is a different idea from the RSI indicator, despite the similar name.
relative-strength.example: Stock +12% and SPY +4% over the same period: the ratio rose about 7.7%.
relative-strength.pitfalls: Outperformance can come from falling less in a down market.

momentum.short: The speed and persistence of a price move. Oscillators such as RSI, MACD and ROC measure it.
momentum.long: Momentum indicators compare recent prices with earlier ones. Rising momentum means moves in one direction are getting stronger; fading momentum means they are slowing even if price is still rising. Momentum is a description, not a forecast.
momentum.example: Price makes a new high but RSI makes a lower high: momentum is fading.
momentum.pitfalls: Momentum readings are noisy on short timeframes.

overbought-oversold.short: Labels for oscillator readings at extremes (for example RSI above 70 or below 30). They describe, they do not predict.
overbought-oversold.long: Overbought means price has risen fast compared with its recent history, oversold that it has fallen fast. Mean-reversion traders treat extremes as stretched; trend traders treat them as signs of strength or weakness. The thresholds are conventions, not laws.
overbought-oversold.example: RSI 78 after a 9-day rally: 'overbought' by the usual definition.
overbought-oversold.pitfalls: Selling every overbought reading in a strong uptrend, or buying every oversold one in a crash, can be very costly.

divergence.short: When price and an indicator disagree, such as a new price high with a lower RSI high.
divergence.long: Bearish divergence is a higher price high with a lower indicator high; bullish divergence is a lower price low with a higher indicator low. It suggests momentum is not confirming the price move. Divergences can last a long time before anything happens, or nothing happens at all.
divergence.example: Highs at 120 then 125, while RSI highs went 74 then 66: bearish divergence.
divergence.pitfalls: Easy to spot after the fact, much harder in real time.

golden-cross.short: Golden cross: a faster moving average crosses above a slower one (classically 50 over 200). Death cross: below.
golden-cross.long: These crossovers are widely reported because they summarise a shift in the medium-term trend against the long-term trend. Because both averages lag, the cross often happens well after the turn in price. This app can alert when a fast/slow pair crosses.
golden-cross.example: The 50-day SMA rises from 98 to 101 while the 200-day is at 100: a golden cross.
golden-cross.pitfalls: In sideways markets the averages cross back and forth repeatedly.

stdev.short: A statistic for how spread out values are around their average. In markets, a basic measure of volatility.
stdev.long: Standard deviation is the square root of the average squared distance from the mean. For normally distributed data about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation and 95% within two. Market returns have fatter tails than a normal distribution, so big moves happen more often than this suggests.
stdev.example: Daily returns averaging 0.05% with a standard deviation of 1.2% imply most days fall between -1.15% and +1.25%.
stdev.pitfalls: It treats up and down moves the same and understates crash risk.

52-week-high.short: The highest and lowest prices of the past year. Widely watched reference levels.
52-week-high.long: Many lists and screeners track stocks near their 52-week high or low. A new 52-week high means the price is above every level of the past year; a new low, below every one. These levels often act as psychological resistance or support.
52-week-high.example: 52-week range 41.20 to 67.80, last 66.10: 2.5% below the 52-week high.
52-week-high.pitfalls: Some sources use closing prices and others intraday highs and lows, so values can differ slightly.

52-week-proximity.short: How far, in percent, the price is below its 52-week high or above its 52-week low.
52-week-proximity.long: Distance from the high = (high - price) / high x 100. Distance from the low = (price - low) / low x 100. An alert on proximity fires when the price comes within a percentage of the extreme.
52-week-proximity.example: High 80, price 76: 5% below the 52-week high. Low 50, price 52: 4% above the 52-week low.
52-week-proximity.pitfalls: Right after a split, unadjusted 52-week values can be meaningless.

price-alert.short: A rule that notifies you when a symbol's price goes above or below a level. It never places an order.
price-alert.long: An alert is a watch, not a trade. In this app, rules run in your browser on each refresh. 'Above' and 'below' fire whenever the condition is true; 'crosses above' and 'crosses below' fire only at the moment of crossing. Optional confirmation needs several consecutive checks before firing.
price-alert.example: Rule: AAPL crosses above 200. It fires once when the price moves from 199.80 to 200.15.
price-alert.pitfalls: Alerts only run while the page is open, and they are only as fresh as your data feed.

crossover.short: The moment one line moves from one side of another to the other, such as price crossing a moving average.
crossover.long: A crossover is detected by comparing the previous and current values: below then above is a cross up, above then below is a cross down. Crossovers mark events, while 'above' and 'below' describe states. Crossover alerts fire once per crossing instead of on every refresh.
crossover.example: Previous: price 99, SMA 100 (below). Now: price 101, SMA 100.2 (above): a cross above.
crossover.pitfalls: Prices that hover around a line produce many crossovers in a row. Confirmation and re-arming settings help.

price-ma-cross.short: Fires when the price crosses above or below a simple or exponential moving average of N bars.
price-ma-cross.long: These alerts compute the moving average from daily bars and compare the live price with it. Crossing the 50- or 200-day average is a common way to watch for a change in trend. The EMA version reacts faster than the SMA version.
price-ma-cross.example: Rule: MSFT crosses below SMA(50). Average 410.20; price drops from 411 to 409.50: alert fires.
price-ma-cross.pitfalls: Needs enough history to compute the average; if bars are unavailable the rule waits instead of guessing.

ma-crossover.short: Fires when a fast moving average crosses a slow one, for example 50 over 200 (golden cross).
ma-crossover.long: The alert watches two averages computed from daily bars. A fast-over-slow cross is often described as bullish and the opposite as bearish, though both are descriptive only. Because they use daily bars, these alerts change at most once per day.
ma-crossover.example: Fast SMA(50) 101.2, slow SMA(200) 100.9, after being below yesterday: alert fires.
ma-crossover.pitfalls: Lagging by design: by the time the averages cross, much of the move may be over.

macd-cross.short: Fires when the MACD line crosses above or below its signal line.
macd-cross.long: The alert computes MACD from daily bars with the usual 12/26/9 settings unless you change them. A cross above is commonly read as momentum turning up, a cross below as turning down.
macd-cross.example: MACD 0.85, signal 0.80 after MACD was below the signal yesterday: cross above.
macd-cross.pitfalls: Frequent crosses in quiet markets; consider combining with a trend filter mentally.

bollinger-break.short: Fires when the price closes outside the upper or lower Bollinger Band.
bollinger-break.long: A close outside a band means the move was large relative to recent volatility, often 2 standard deviations. This alert describes the event; it says nothing about whether the move will continue or reverse.
bollinger-break.example: Upper band 53.10; price trades at 53.40: alert 'above upper band' fires.
bollinger-break.pitfalls: In strong trends this can fire day after day; consider the 'once' repeat mode.

atr-move.short: Fires when today's move from the previous close is bigger than k times the ATR.
atr-move.long: Instead of a fixed percentage, this alert scales to each symbol's normal volatility. A 2 x ATR move is unusual for that particular symbol, whether it is a calm utility or a volatile tech stock.
atr-move.example: ATR(14) 1.50, k = 2: alert fires if the price moves more than 3.00 from the previous close.
atr-move.pitfalls: After a very volatile period, ATR is inflated and the alert becomes harder to trigger.

trailing-stop.short: A level that follows the price up by a fixed percentage below its highest point and never moves down.
trailing-stop.long: A trailing stop rises with the price but stays put when the price falls. When price drops a set percentage from its peak, it triggers. In this app it is an alert, not an order: it tracks the highest price since the rule was armed and tells you when the drop is reached.
trailing-stop.example: Trail 10%. Armed at 50, price rises to 60 (stop moves to 54), then falls to 53.90: the alert fires.
trailing-stop.pitfalls: Too tight a trail triggers on normal noise. Data gaps and delays mean the alert can fire after the actual level was crossed.

alert-repeat.short: Whether an alert disarms after firing ('once') or re-arms to fire again when the condition resets ('re-arm').
alert-repeat.long: With 'once', the rule fires a single time and then stays off until you arm it again. With 're-arm', it fires, waits until the condition is no longer true, then can fire again. Rules can also have an expiry date.
alert-repeat.example: Re-arm rule 'price above 100': fires at 100.20, resets when price drops to 99, fires again at 100.10.
alert-repeat.pitfalls: Re-arm on a level the price hovers around can produce a stream of notifications; use 'once' or confirmation.

alert-confirmation.short: Requires the condition to hold on several consecutive refreshes before firing, filtering out brief spikes.
alert-confirmation.long: Confirmation trades speed for reliability. With 3 ticks of confirmation and a 15-second refresh, a condition must hold for about 45 seconds. That filters one-off bad prints and momentary wicks.
alert-confirmation.example: Rule: below 48, confirm 3. Price dips to 47.90 for one refresh then recovers: no alert.

portfolio-alert.short: Rules on the whole portfolio: total value, today's profit/loss in money, or today's percentage change.
portfolio-alert.long: Portfolio alerts use your recorded holdings and the latest quotes. They are useful for keeping an eye on overall risk instead of individual symbols. If some quotes are missing or currencies cannot be converted, the totals are partial and the alert says so.
portfolio-alert.example: Rule: portfolio day change below -3%. Holdings fall 3.2% in total: alert fires.
portfolio-alert.pitfalls: Totals are only as accurate as your ledger and the currency conversion.

day-pl.short: How much a position or portfolio gained or lost today, measured from the previous close.
day-pl.long: Day P/L = quantity x (last price - previous close), summed over positions. For positions bought today it should be measured from the purchase price instead. Day P/L % divides by yesterday's value.
day-pl.example: 100 shares, prev close 40.00, last 41.20: day P/L +120.
day-pl.pitfalls: Mixed currencies must be converted before adding up.

earnings-report.short: A company's quarterly results: revenue, profit and EPS, often with guidance. Prices can jump sharply on them.
earnings-report.long: Public companies report results each quarter. Analysts publish estimates beforehand, and the price reaction depends on results versus those expectations and on guidance for the future. Reports are often released before the open or after the close, causing gaps.
earnings-report.example: EPS estimate 1.10, actual 1.25: a 'beat' of 0.15. The stock may still fall if revenue or guidance disappoints.
earnings-report.pitfalls: Holding through earnings exposes you to large overnight gaps.

eps.short: A company's net profit divided by its shares outstanding.
eps.long: EPS tells you how much profit each share represents. Trailing EPS (TTM) uses the last four quarters; forward EPS uses analysts' estimates. Diluted EPS counts options and convertibles as if exercised.
eps.pitfalls: One-off gains or charges can distort EPS. Buybacks raise EPS without the business growing.

pe.short: Price divided by earnings per share: how many years of current profit the market is paying for.
pe.long: P/E = share price / EPS (usually trailing 12 months). A higher P/E often reflects expectations of faster growth, or a pricier stock. P/E is most useful compared with the company's own history and with similar companies in the same industry.
pe.pitfalls: Meaningless when earnings are negative or tiny. A low P/E can mean a business in decline.

forward-pe.short: Price divided by expected EPS for the next 12 months or fiscal year.
forward-pe.long: Forward P/E uses analyst estimates instead of reported results. If it is lower than the trailing P/E, earnings are expected to grow. It is only as good as the estimates.
forward-pe.example: Price 60, next-year EPS estimate 5: forward P/E = 12.
forward-pe.pitfalls: Estimates are often revised and tend to be optimistic.

peg.short: P/E divided by the expected earnings growth rate. A rough way to put valuation next to growth.
peg.long: PEG = P/E / annual EPS growth (in percent). A PEG near 1 is sometimes described as growth being 'fairly priced', but that is a rule of thumb. Different sources use different growth periods.
peg.pitfalls: Growth estimates over several years are highly uncertain.

ps.short: Market cap divided by annual revenue. Used when a company has little or no profit.
ps.long: Price-to-sales compares the company's value with its sales. It works for companies that are not yet profitable, but it ignores costs completely. Typical levels vary hugely by industry.
ps.example: Market cap 10 billion, revenue 2.5 billion: P/S = 4.
ps.pitfalls: High revenue with no path to profit can still be a poor business.

pb.short: Share price divided by book value (assets minus liabilities) per share.
pb.long: Price-to-book compares market value with accounting net worth. It is most often used for banks and asset-heavy businesses. Many valuable companies have most of their value in intangible things that book value does not count.
pb.example: Price 30, book value per share 20: P/B = 1.5.
pb.pitfalls: Book value can be outdated or distorted by write-downs and buybacks.

dividend.short: A cash payment a company makes to shareholders, usually from profits, often quarterly.
dividend.long: Dividends are declared by a company's board and are not guaranteed. On the ex-dividend date the share price typically drops by roughly the dividend amount. Dividends may be taxed and may have withholding taxes when paid across borders.
dividend.example: 0.50 per share quarterly; holding 200 shares pays 100 per quarter before taxes.
dividend.pitfalls: A dividend does not create value by itself: the price adjusts down by about the amount paid.

dividend-yield.short: Annual dividends per share divided by the share price, as a percentage.
dividend-yield.long: Yield = annual dividend / price x 100. Because price is the denominator, yield rises when the price falls. Trailing yield uses dividends already paid; forward yield uses the announced rate.
dividend-yield.pitfalls: A very high yield often signals the market expects a dividend cut.

payout-ratio.short: The share of earnings paid out as dividends.
payout-ratio.long: Payout ratio = dividends per share / EPS. A low ratio leaves room to keep or raise the dividend; a ratio above 100% means paying out more than the company earns. Real estate trusts and some utilities normally have high ratios.
payout-ratio.pitfalls: Based on accounting earnings, which can differ from cash flow.

ex-dividend-date.short: You must own the shares before this date to receive the next dividend.
ex-dividend-date.long: Buying on or after the ex-date means the seller keeps that dividend. The share price usually opens lower on the ex-date by about the dividend amount. The payment date comes later, often weeks after.
ex-dividend-date.example: Ex-date 12 March, pay date 1 April: shares bought on 11 March (and held) receive the dividend; shares bought on 12 March do not.
ex-dividend-date.pitfalls: Buying just before the ex-date to 'capture' a dividend usually does not work after the price drop and taxes.

stock-split.short: A company divides each share into several (or merges several into one). Value is unchanged; only the count and price change.
stock-split.long: In a 4-for-1 split each share becomes four, and the price is divided by four. A reverse split does the opposite and is often done by companies whose price has fallen very low. Charts are usually adjusted backwards so the split does not look like a crash.
stock-split.example: Holding 10 shares at 400 before a 4:1 split: after it, 40 shares at about 100. Still worth 4,000.
stock-split.pitfalls: Record splits in your ledger, or your share count and cost per share will be wrong.

beta.short: How much a stock has tended to move compared with the market. 1 = like the market, 2 = twice as much.
beta.long: Beta is estimated by regressing the stock's returns on an index's returns, often over 5 years of monthly data. A beta above 1 means bigger swings than the market in both directions; below 1, smaller swings. Negative beta means it tended to move the opposite way.
beta.example: Beta 1.5: when the index fell 10%, the stock fell about 15% on average.
beta.pitfalls: Beta is backward-looking and changes over time; it ignores company-specific risk.

roe.short: Net income divided by shareholders' equity: how much profit the company makes with owners' money.
roe.long: ROE = net income / shareholders' equity. Higher ROE means more profit per unit of capital the owners put in. Debt can raise ROE artificially, so read it together with debt/equity.
roe.pitfalls: Buybacks shrink equity and can make ROE look better without a better business.

profit-margin.short: The share of revenue left as profit. Gross, operating and net margins measure it at different stages.
profit-margin.long: Gross margin subtracts direct costs; operating margin also subtracts running costs; net margin is what remains after everything, including interest and taxes. Margins are best compared within the same industry.
profit-margin.example: Revenue 1 billion, net income 80M: net margin 8%.
profit-margin.pitfalls: One-off items can swing net margin sharply in a single quarter.

revenue-growth.short: How fast a company's sales are increasing, usually year over year.
revenue-growth.long: Revenue growth compares sales with the same period a year earlier, which removes seasonal effects. It shows demand for the business, but not whether that demand is profitable. Acquisitions can inflate it.
revenue-growth.example: Revenue 1.2 billion this year vs 1.0 billion last year: 20% growth.
revenue-growth.pitfalls: Currency moves affect revenue reported by multinational companies.

debt-to-equity.short: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity: how much the company relies on borrowing.
debt-to-equity.long: A higher ratio means more financial leverage, which magnifies both returns and risk. Interest costs rise with debt and interest rates. Banks and utilities normally run higher ratios than software companies.
debt-to-equity.pitfalls: Providers define debt differently (with or without leases), so values vary between sources.

fundamentals.short: Business data about a company, such as earnings, revenue, margins, debt and dividends, as opposed to price charts.
fundamentals.long: Fundamental analysis looks at what a business earns and owns to judge its value. Technical analysis looks at price and volume behaviour. Many investors use both. Fundamentals change quarterly, while prices change every second.
fundamentals.example: P/E, dividend yield and debt/equity are fundamental ratios; RSI and MACD are technical indicators.
fundamentals.pitfalls: Free providers update fundamentals with a delay and sometimes with errors.

cost-basis.short: What you paid for a position, including fees. Profit and loss are measured against it.
cost-basis.long: Cost basis = shares x price paid + commissions. When you buy several times, each purchase is a lot with its own basis. Splits change the per-share basis but not the total. Tax rules decide how basis is assigned when you sell part of a position.
cost-basis.example: Bought 50 at 20 with a 5 fee: cost basis = 1,005, or 20.10 per share.
cost-basis.pitfalls: Forgetting fees or splits gives a wrong basis and wrong P/L.

lot.short: One purchase of a security, with its own date, quantity and price.
lot.long: If you buy the same stock three times, you hold three lots. When you sell, the method you (or your tax rules) use decides which lots are sold, which changes realized gains. Lots also determine holding periods.
lot.example: Lot 1: 10 shares at 100 in January. Lot 2: 10 shares at 120 in June.
lot.pitfalls: Brokers and tax authorities may use a different lot method from the one you choose here.

fifo.short: When you sell, the oldest shares are considered sold first.
fifo.long: FIFO matches each sale against your earliest open lots. In a rising market it usually produces larger realized gains, because the oldest shares tend to be the cheapest. FIFO is the default in many tax systems.
fifo.example: Lots: 10 at 100 then 10 at 120. Sell 10 at 130 under FIFO: realized gain = 10 x (130 - 100) = 300.
fifo.pitfalls: Your country's tax rules may require a specific method. This app's figures are informational, not tax reports.

average-cost.short: Every share has the same cost: the total paid divided by the total shares held.
average-cost.long: With average cost, each sale uses the weighted average price of all shares held. Buying more shares changes the average; selling does not. Mexico, for example, uses an inflation-adjusted average cost for tax purposes.
average-cost.example: 10 at 100 plus 10 at 120: average cost 110. Sell 10 at 130: realized gain = 10 x (130 - 110) = 200.
average-cost.pitfalls: Average cost and FIFO give different realized P/L for the same trades.

unrealized-pl.short: Profit or loss on positions you still hold: current value minus cost basis. It changes with every price move.
unrealized-pl.long: Unrealized ('paper') P/L becomes realized only when you sell. It is shown both in money and as a percentage of cost basis. It ignores dividends already received unless you add them separately.
unrealized-pl.example: Cost basis 1,005; 50 shares now at 23 = 1,150: unrealized P/L +145 (+14.4%).
unrealized-pl.pitfalls: Taxes and selling costs are not deducted, so the figure overstates what you would keep.

realized-pl.short: Profit or loss locked in by selling: sale proceeds minus the cost basis of the shares sold.
realized-pl.long: Realized P/L is what tax reports usually care about. It depends on which lots were sold (FIFO or average cost) and includes selling fees. Once realized, later price moves no longer affect it.
realized-pl.example: Sell 20 shares at 25 with a 5 fee (proceeds 495); their basis was 402: realized gain 93.
realized-pl.pitfalls: A realized loss is still a loss; selling winners and keeping losers can feel good but shifts risk.

total-return.short: Price change plus dividends and other income, minus fees, over a period.
total-return.long: Total return gives the full picture of what an investment earned. A stock flat in price but paying 4% dividends had a total return near 4%. Comparing with a benchmark should also use the benchmark's total return.
total-return.example: Bought 1,000, now worth 1,080, received 30 in dividends, paid 5 in fees: total return 105, or 10.5%.
total-return.pitfalls: Price-only charts understate the returns of dividend-paying assets.

yield-on-cost.short: Annual dividends divided by what you originally paid, not the current price.
yield-on-cost.long: Yield on cost rises if a company grows its dividend while you hold it. It is a personal measure of income relative to your investment, not a measure of the stock's current attractiveness.
yield-on-cost.example: Bought at 40, annual dividend now 2.40: yield on cost 6%, while the current yield at a price of 80 is 3%.
yield-on-cost.pitfalls: A high yield on cost says nothing about whether keeping the money in that stock still makes sense.

allocation.short: How your portfolio is divided: by asset class, sector, country, currency or account.
allocation.long: Allocation shows where your money actually is. Two portfolios with the same total can carry very different risks depending on how concentrated they are. Many investors set target percentages and check how far they have drifted.
allocation.example: 60% stocks, 30% bonds, 10% cash; or by sector: 45% technology, 20% health care, 35% other.
allocation.pitfalls: ETFs can hide concentration: three different index funds may hold the same top companies.

drift.short: How far each holding's current weight has moved from its target weight.
drift.long: Prices move, so weights move. Drift = current weight - target weight. Watching drift shows when a portfolio no longer matches its plan, without suggesting what to do about it.
drift.example: Target 20% in a fund; it rose and is now 26% of the portfolio: drift +6 percentage points.
drift.pitfalls: Small drifts are normal; reacting to every percentage point means more trading costs and taxes.

rebalancing.short: Bringing a portfolio's weights back to target, usually by trimming what grew and adding to what shrank.
rebalancing.long: Rebalancing keeps risk close to what you planned. Common approaches are by calendar (once a year) or by threshold (when drift exceeds a set amount). It can be done with new contributions to avoid selling.
rebalancing.example: Target 60/40 stocks/bonds, now 70/30: rebalancing would move 10% of the portfolio from stocks to bonds.
rebalancing.pitfalls: Selling can trigger taxes and fees. This app only shows drift; it does not place trades.

diversification.short: Spreading money across different assets so one bad outcome does not sink the whole portfolio.
diversification.long: Holdings that do not move together reduce overall volatility. Diversification works across companies, sectors, countries, asset classes and currencies. It reduces company-specific risk but not market-wide risk.
diversification.example: One stock can fall 60% after bad news; a fund of 500 stocks rarely falls that much because of one company.
diversification.pitfalls: Owning many stocks in the same sector is not real diversification. Correlations rise in crises.

base-currency.short: The currency your portfolio totals are shown in. Holdings in other currencies are converted with FX rates.
base-currency.long: If you live in Mexico and own US stocks, your base currency is probably MXN. Your return then includes both the stock's move and the USD/MXN move. If a conversion rate is missing, totals are marked partial instead of mixing currencies.
base-currency.example: 100 shares at 50 USD with USDMXN 18.20: 91,000 MXN in base currency.
base-currency.pitfalls: Adding USD and MXN amounts without converting gives meaningless totals.

currency-risk.short: The chance that exchange-rate moves change the value of foreign investments in your own currency.
currency-risk.long: A foreign stock can rise in its own currency while falling in yours, or the reverse. Currency risk affects both prices and dividends. Some ETFs hedge it, at a cost.
currency-risk.example: A US stock rises 5% in USD, but USDMXN falls from 18.00 to 17.10 (-5%): for a peso investor the gain is about 0%.
currency-risk.pitfalls: Over short periods, currency moves can be larger than the stock moves.

cash.short: Uninvested money in your accounts. It counts in your net worth and allocation.
cash.long: Cash comes from deposits, sales, dividends and interest, and goes out through purchases, fees, taxes and withdrawals. Tracking it per currency makes returns and allocation accurate.
cash.example: Deposit 10,000, buy 6,000 of stock, receive 50 in dividends: cash 4,050.
cash.pitfalls: Leaving cash out of the ledger makes the portfolio look riskier and more concentrated than it is.

net-worth.short: Market value of all positions plus cash, converted to your base currency.
net-worth.long: This is the total of what you hold, at current prices. It goes up and down with the market and with deposits and withdrawals. That is why returns are measured with methods like TWR and XIRR, which separate investment performance from money you added or removed.
net-worth.pitfalls: A higher value after a deposit is not a gain. Use return measures to judge performance.

xirr.short: Your personal annualised return, taking into account when and how much money you put in or took out.
xirr.long: XIRR finds the yearly rate that makes all your dated cash flows (deposits negative, withdrawals and final value positive) add up to zero. It rewards or punishes the timing of your contributions. It is the right measure for 'how did my money do?'.
xirr.example: Invest 1,000 on 1 Jan, 1,000 more on 1 Jul, worth 2,150 on 31 Dec: XIRR is about 10%, higher than the simple 7.5% because half the money was invested for only half a year.
xirr.pitfalls: Over very short periods annualised returns can look absurd (a 2% gain in a week annualises to over 180%).

twr.short: Return that removes the effect of deposits and withdrawals, so you can compare with a benchmark or fund.
twr.long: TWR splits the period at every cash flow, measures the return of each sub-period, and chains them together. Fund managers report TWR because they do not control when clients add money. Compare TWR with an index's return to judge your selections.
twr.example: Sub-period returns +10% then -5%: TWR = 1.10 x 0.95 - 1 = +4.5%, whatever amounts were deposited in between.
twr.pitfalls: Needs portfolio values at each cash-flow date; missing prices make it approximate.

benchmark.short: A reference index or fund used to judge performance, such as the S&P 500 or the IPC.
benchmark.long: A benchmark answers 'compared with what?'. The fair benchmark resembles what you hold: a portfolio of Mexican stocks against the S&P/BMV IPC, a global portfolio against a world index. Use total return for both.
benchmark.example: Your TWR +8% vs S&P 500 total return +11%: you underperformed by 3 percentage points.
benchmark.pitfalls: Choosing a benchmark after the fact to look good defeats the purpose.

volatility.short: How much returns swing around their average. Usually annualised standard deviation of returns.
volatility.long: Higher volatility means bigger ups and downs. Daily volatility is annualised by multiplying by the square root of about 252 trading days. Volatility is a common proxy for risk, though it treats sharp gains the same as sharp losses.
volatility.example: Daily standard deviation 1.5%: annualised volatility about 1.5% x 15.9 = 23.8%.
volatility.pitfalls: Calm periods underestimate the risk of a sudden crash.

sharpe.short: Return above the risk-free rate, divided by volatility. Higher means more return per unit of risk.
sharpe.long: Sharpe = (portfolio return - risk-free rate) / volatility, usually annualised. It allows comparison of strategies with different risk levels. Values above 1 over long periods are generally considered good.
sharpe.pitfalls: Short histories give unreliable Sharpe ratios; it also penalises upside volatility.

sortino.short: Like the Sharpe ratio, but only counts downside volatility as risk.
sortino.long: Sortino = (return - target) / downside deviation, where downside deviation looks only at returns below the target. It does not penalise strong upside moves, which some investors prefer.
sortino.pitfalls: With few negative periods, downside deviation is poorly estimated.

drawdown.short: The drop from a previous peak to a later low. Max drawdown is the worst such drop in a period.
drawdown.long: Drawdown measures pain: how much was lost from the high point before recovering. Max drawdown is a key risk statistic because it shows the worst experience an investor would have had. Recovery needs a bigger percentage gain than the loss.
drawdown.example: Peak 120,000, low 84,000: drawdown -30%. Getting back to 120,000 needs +42.9%.
drawdown.pitfalls: Past max drawdown is not the worst possible; future ones can be deeper.

correlation.short: How closely two assets' returns move together, from -1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to +1 (in step).
correlation.long: Correlation is computed on returns, not prices. Low or negative correlation between holdings is what makes diversification work. Correlations change over time and tend to rise in market panics.
correlation.example: Two bank stocks might have a correlation of 0.85; a stock and a government bond fund might be near 0 or negative.
correlation.pitfalls: Correlation measures linear co-movement and says nothing about cause.

alpha.short: Return beyond what beta and the benchmark would explain. Positive alpha means outperformance after adjusting for market risk.
alpha.long: Alpha = actual return - (risk-free rate + beta x (benchmark return - risk-free rate)). It tries to isolate skill or specific factors from simple market exposure. Over short periods, alpha is mostly noise.
alpha.example: Return 14%, risk-free 4%, beta 1.2, benchmark 10%: expected 4 + 1.2 x 6 = 11.2%, alpha +2.8%.
alpha.pitfalls: Depends heavily on the benchmark chosen and the time period.

position-size.short: Deciding how many shares to hold so that a loss to your stop would cost only a set share of your account.
position-size.long: A common educational formula: shares = (account x risk %) / (entry - stop). It ties the size of each position to how far away your exit is, so wide stops mean smaller positions. Fees and slippage should be included.
position-size.example: Account 50,000, risk 1% (500), entry 40, stop 37: 500 / 3 = 166 shares (about 6,640 invested).
position-size.pitfalls: Gaps can blow through a stop, so the real loss can exceed the planned amount. Educational calculation, not advice.

stop-loss.short: A pre-decided exit price that limits the loss on a position. Here it can be watched with an alert; this app does not place orders.
stop-loss.long: At a broker, a stop order becomes a market order when the stop price is touched. Stops are often placed beyond a support level or a multiple of ATR from the entry. A stop defines the risk used in position sizing and risk/reward.
stop-loss.example: Entry 40, stop 37: planned risk 3 per share (7.5%).
stop-loss.pitfalls: A stop is not guaranteed: in a gap the fill can be far below the stop. Stops set too close trigger on normal noise.

risk-reward.short: Potential gain to a target divided by potential loss to a stop.
risk-reward.long: Reward/risk = (target - entry) / (entry - stop). A ratio of 2 means the target is twice as far as the stop. The win rate needed to break even is 1 / (1 + ratio), before fees.
risk-reward.example: Entry 40, stop 37, target 46: reward 6, risk 3, ratio 2:1. Break-even win rate = 1 / 3 = 33%.
risk-reward.pitfalls: A high ratio with a target that is very unlikely to be reached is not better. Educational calculation, not advice.

r-multiple.short: A result expressed in units of the initial risk (R). Gaining twice what you risked is +2R.
r-multiple.long: R is the amount you planned to lose if the stop was hit. Measuring results in R makes trades of different sizes comparable and shows whether losses are kept to about -1R. The average R across many trades is called expectancy.
r-multiple.example: Risk 3 per share. Exit at 44.50 from an entry of 40: +4.5 / 3 = +1.5R.
r-multiple.pitfalls: Needs an honest initial stop; moving stops after entry makes R meaningless.

break-even.short: The price at which a position neither gains nor loses after fees.
break-even.long: Break-even = (cost basis + selling fees) / shares for a long position. With round-trip fees and spreads, the price must rise a little above your purchase price just to break even.
break-even.example: Bought 100 at 20 with 5 fee, will pay 5 to sell: break-even = (2,005 + 5) / 100 = 20.10.
break-even.pitfalls: Taxes on gains move the after-tax break-even further.

leverage.short: Using borrowed money (margin) or leveraged products to control more than you own. Gains and losses are magnified.
leverage.long: With 2x leverage, a 10% drop in the asset is a 20% loss of your money, plus interest. Brokers can force-sell positions (a margin call) if your equity falls below a minimum, often at the worst time. Leveraged ETFs and CFDs carry similar risks and their own decay.
leverage.example: 10,000 of your own plus 10,000 borrowed, all in a stock that drops 30%: position 14,000, debt 10,000, your equity 4,000 (-60%).
leverage.pitfalls: Losses can exceed your deposit. This app only monitors; it does not offer margin or leveraged trading.

short-selling.short: Selling borrowed shares to profit if the price falls. Losses are theoretically unlimited.
short-selling.long: A short seller borrows shares, sells them, and later buys them back to return. If the price rises instead, the loss grows without a cap. Short sellers also pay borrow fees and any dividends paid while short.
short-selling.example: Short at 50, buy back at 40: gain 10 per share. Buy back at 80: loss 30 per share.
short-selling.pitfalls: Short squeezes can force rapid buying and huge losses.

fees.short: Commissions, spreads, fund expenses, FX conversion and custody fees. They reduce every return.
