fees.long: Costs are certain while returns are not. Small, frequent costs, such as commissions on many small trades, add up. Currency conversion fees can be large for investors buying foreign stocks.
fees.example: 10 trades a month at a 5 fee each on a 10,000 account costs 600 a year: 6% before any gain.
fees.pitfalls: 'Zero commission' brokers may still earn on spreads, FX or cash.

taxes.short: Gains, dividends and interest are usually taxable. Rules depend on your country, account type and holding period.
taxes.long: Many countries tax realized gains, not unrealized ones. Some distinguish short- and long-term holdings; some have tax-advantaged retirement accounts. Dividends from foreign companies may have tax withheld at source. Brokers issue official tax statements, and those take precedence over any app.
taxes.example: In Mexico, gains on listed shares sold through a local broker usually pay a 10% rate on the net gain; other countries differ.
taxes.pitfalls: This app's numbers are informational. Ask a qualified tax professional about your situation.

fomo.short: The urge to buy something because it has already risen sharply and others are profiting.
fomo.long: FOMO tends to strike late in a move, when prices are already high and volatility is rising. Chasing makes people skip their own plan for entry, size and exit. Pre-defined rules and alerts can help slow decisions down.
fomo.example: A stock is up 40% in three days and trending on social media; buying because of that is a FOMO decision.
fomo.pitfalls: Feeling certain is not evidence. Ask what would make you wrong before acting.

overtrading.short: Trading too often or too large, usually driven by emotion. Costs and mistakes add up quickly.
overtrading.long: Frequent trading increases commissions, spreads and taxes, and makes each decision less careful. Watching a live screen all day can encourage it. Many experienced investors trade rarely and monitor with alerts instead.
overtrading.example: Twenty round trips a month, each costing 0.2% in spread and fees, costs about 48% of the account a year if the whole account turns over each time.
overtrading.pitfalls: Activity feels productive but is not the same as progress.

delayed-data.short: Prices shown with a lag (often 15 minutes, sometimes more) because real-time exchange data costs money.
delayed-data.long: Exchanges charge for real-time feeds, so free plans often provide delayed or partial data. Some providers give real-time prices from a single venue, which may differ slightly from the consolidated market. This app shows the quote time and marks stale data so you know what you are looking at.
delayed-data.example: At 10:30 a 15-minute delayed quote shows the price as it was at 10:15.
delayed-data.pitfalls: Alerts on delayed data fire late. Never treat a delayed price as tradable.

real-time-data.short: Prices delivered within seconds of the trade. Usually requires a paid plan or a broker's own feed.
real-time-data.long: Even 'real-time' data passes through networks and polling intervals. In this browser app, quotes are refreshed on an interval (for example every 15 seconds), so there is always some delay. Single-exchange real-time feeds may show slightly different prices from the consolidated tape.
real-time-data.example: With a 15-second refresh, a quote can be up to about 15 seconds old plus network time.
real-time-data.pitfalls: Faster refresh uses up free API quotas sooner.

stale-quote.short: A price whose timestamp has stopped advancing. The market may be closed or halted, or the feed may have stalled.
stale-quote.long: This app watches how long each quote's timestamp has stayed the same. If it stops updating during a session when it should be moving, the quote is flagged stale rather than presented as current.
stale-quote.example: Session open, but MSFT's quote time has been 10:02 for 12 minutes: shown as stale.
stale-quote.pitfalls: A quiet stock can look stale even when the feed is fine.

data-provider.short: The service the app fetches prices from, using your own API key. Each has different coverage, delays and limits.
data-provider.long: This app connects directly from your browser to providers such as Finnhub, Twelve Data, Alpha Vantage, Polygon or Alpaca. Your keys stay on your device. Providers differ in which exchanges, crypto and FX they cover, and in whether data is real-time or delayed.
data-provider.example: One provider may cover US stocks in real time but not Mexican ones; another covers BMV with a delay.
data-provider.pitfalls: If a provider cannot cover a symbol, the app says so instead of showing a made-up price.

api-key.short: A personal code that identifies you to a data provider. Treat it like a password.
api-key.long: Free API keys are available from most providers after signing up. In this app keys are stored only in your browser. Anyone with your key can use your quota.
api-key.example: Paste a free Finnhub key in Settings to switch from demo data to live quotes.
api-key.pitfalls: Do not share screenshots or exported files that include your key.

rate-limit.short: The maximum number of requests a provider allows per minute or per day. Exceeding it pauses data.
rate-limit.long: Free plans are limited, such as a set number of calls per minute or per day. Watching many symbols at a fast refresh uses the quota quickly. This app paces requests and shows a usage meter.
rate-limit.example: With a limit of 8 requests per minute and 20 symbols, a full refresh takes about 3 minutes unless batch requests are available.
rate-limit.pitfalls: Charts and fundamentals also use quota, not just quotes.

demo-data.short: Simulated prices for learning the app without an API key. Not real market data.
demo-data.long: Demo mode generates realistic-looking but synthetic quotes and charts so you can explore every feature. It is clearly labelled with a 'Demo' chip. Never use demo values for any real decision.
demo-data.example: Without a key, AAPL shows a simulated price that may be far from the actual market price.
demo-data.pitfalls: If a live provider cannot supply a chart, the app labels any fallback as demo data rather than mixing it in silently.

watchlist.short: Your list of symbols to follow. It is the starting point for quotes, charts and alerts.
watchlist.long: A watchlist keeps the symbols you care about in one place, sorted by whatever matters to you. Adding a symbol to a watchlist does not buy it; it only monitors it.
watchlist.example: A starter watchlist could hold SPY (US market), an ETF you own, a currency pair like USDMXN and one stock you are researching.
watchlist.pitfalls: Watching too many symbols at once makes everything harder to see and uses more API quota.

screener.short: A filter that lists symbols matching conditions, such as 'RSI below 30 and price above SMA(200)'.
screener.long: A screener scans a set of symbols and shows those meeting your criteria. Presets are a starting point for research, not recommendations. Results depend on the data available for each symbol.
screener.example: Screen: within 5% of a 52-week high AND relative volume above 2.
screener.pitfalls: A screen shows what matched, not why or what will happen next. Educational, not advice.

class-shares.short: Different kinds of shares in the same company, often with different voting rights, shown by a letter after the ticker.
class-shares.long: Some companies issue more than one class of stock. Class A and class B shares may carry different votes or different prices, but they usually own a slice of the same business. Providers write the class differently: BRK.B, BRK-B and BRK/B can all mean Berkshire Hathaway class B. Alphabet trades as GOOGL (class A, votes) and GOOG (class C, no votes).
class-shares.example: BRK.A trades for hundreds of thousands of dollars a share and BRK.B for a few hundred; one A share converts into 1,500 B shares.
class-shares.pitfalls: If a symbol shows 'Not covered', try the other spelling of the class (a dot, a dash or a slash). Do not compare the prices of two classes as if they were the same share.

crypto-pair-notation.short: Crypto prices are quoted against another currency, written as COIN-USD or COINUSD; a bare ticker may be a company instead.
crypto-pair-notation.long: A crypto price is always a pair: bitcoin in US dollars is BTC-USD (or BTCUSD). Here a bare coin ticker such as BTC or ETH is treated as the coin, except where a listed company uses the same letters — LINK, DASH or COMP are stocks unless you write LINK-USD. Search suggests the pair form for you.
crypto-pair-notation.example: Typing LINK adds the company with that ticker; typing LINK-USD adds the Chainlink coin priced in dollars.
crypto-pair-notation.pitfalls: The same coin can have slightly different prices on different venues and providers. Check the source shown next to the price.
